questions.prompt: When does backtracking abandon (prune) a partial solution?

options.text: As soon as it cannot possibly lead to a valid complete solution
Only after building every complete candidate
Never — it explores the entire search space

questions.explanation: Backtracking prunes a branch the moment a partial candidate violates a constraint, avoiding the exponential work of exploring it fully.

questions.prompt: What is the size of the search space when generating all subsets of n elements?
questions.explanation: Each element is independently in or out of a subset, giving 2ⁿ subsets. (Permutations, by contrast, number n!.)

questions.prompt: Which statements about backtracking are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It builds solutions incrementally, one choice at a time
Pruning invalid branches early is what makes it practical
It explores via recursion and undoes each choice (un-choose)

questions.explanation: Backtracking is incremental, prunes early, and follows choose/explore/un-choose. Its worst case is exponential, so (d) is false.

questions.prompt: Abandoning a partial candidate that cannot lead to a valid solution is called ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Pruning cuts off branches of the search tree that violate constraints, which is what keeps an exponential search tractable.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the backtracking template for one choice.
questions.explanation: For each option you choose it, explore recursively, undo it to restore state, then move on to the next option.

questions.prompt: Match each item with its fact.

pairs.right: Place one queen per row, prune attacks

questions.explanation: The combinatorial sizes are exponential; N-Queens is the classic pruned search; the template ties it all together.
